items.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And us jazz musicians from Louis Armstrong to Coltrane to Don Cherry and Ornette

ctx.x: Yes. Because God, if you believe in God, whatever you believe, if God wants to give you a gift he wraps it in a problem. And so I think we’ve been given a gift and we’ve been made to look at ourselves and look at our actions, and we can either see and learn the lessons from those, but we’ve had problems all this whole time that we’ve ignored. And there’s a saying that says that problem that you have is now two, is now three, because you ignored it, now four because you ignored it. And it begins to grow…

your response? So one thing about artists is we do have feelings. And we express them generally through music but we also — it’s necessary for us to take a stand verbally and to language through our art but also verbally. So “shut up and dribble” that’s slave stuff. Right? When somebody tells you, “Yeah you guys get beaten when you get stopped by the police, that’s ‘cause you’re not acting like you’re supposed to act.” You know how they want you to act? Like a slave. “Yessir boss, I’s sorry. Here’s my license.”…
You can play your horn. Sing for me boy. But they don’t want you to have an opinion about something. And I’ve got opinions. And my opinions aren’t wrong.

items.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: So we started playing “When You’re Smiling” and it started me listening to Louis again.

ctx.x: There’s a lot of music in college that you won’t play anywhere else, because the music just takes so long to prepare. In other words, not to get on another tangent, it’s about time when you get in a professional arena, if you go to the Chicago Symphony, well let me give a better example. When you go play a show somewhere, they’re going to try and make the music not so difficult because they might have an hour, two hours at the most, to rehearse it. They can’t give you a bunch of incredibly hard stuff, they’re…

watching how he integrated entertainment into the whole thing was interesting. And then Lionel was the first guy, we’re running a little short here, but Lionel was the first guy that he heard me playing and he said, “Yeah sometimes you sound like Louis Armstrong.” And I had had a little, I always loved Louis, but he wasn’t like my main thing, my man was Kenny Dorham and Lee Morgan. But I always loved Louis Armstrong. He said, “You know I recorded with Louis Armstrong.” I said, “Of course, I know.” He said, “Let’s…
I had heard it in your playing last night every once in a while.
